{{short description|American mathematician}}
{{Use American English|date=March 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2026}}
'''Morton Landers Curtis''' (November 11, 1921 – February 4, 1989)<ref>{{cite web|last=Curtis|first=Morton L.|title=Morton L. Curtis|url=http://www.genealogybank.com/gbnk/ssdi/doc/ssdi/v1:1130C608D456AE28|publisher=Genealogy Bank|access-date=30 October 2013}}</ref> was an American mathematician, an expert on [[group theory]] and the [[William Lewis Moody, Jr.|W. L. Moody, Jr.]] Professor of Mathematics at [[Rice University]].<ref name="ruga">[http://scholarship.rice.edu/bitstream/handle/1911/36025/riceuniversityge196869hous.pdf?sequence=1 Rice University General Announcements for the Academic Year 1968–1969], retrieved 2011-07-13.</ref>

Born in [[Texas]],<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cpkiAQAAMAAJ&q=%22Curtis,+Morton+Landers%22 |title=American men and women of science ... - Jaques Cattell Press - Google Books |year=1982 |via=[[Google Books]]|access-date=2012-01-05}}</ref> Curtis earned a bachelor's degree in 1948 from [[Texas A&M University–Kingsville|Texas A&I University]],<ref name="ruga"/> and received his Ph.D. in 1951 from the [[University of Michigan]] under the supervision of [[Raymond Louis Wilder]]. Subsequently, he taught mathematics at [[Florida State University]] before moving to Rice. At Rice, he was the Ph.D. advisor of well-known mathematician [[John Morgan (mathematician)|John Morgan]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=Morton L. Curtis|id=5144}}</ref>

Curtis is, with [[James J. Andrews (mathematician)|James J. Andrews]], the namesake of the [[Andrews–Curtis conjecture]] concerning [[Nielsen transformation]]s of balanced [[Presentation of a group|group presentations]]. Andrews and Curtis formulated the conjecture in a 1965 paper;<ref>{{Citation | last1=Andrews | first1=James J. |author-link1=James J. Andrews (mathematician)| last2=Curtis | first2=Morton L. | title=Free groups and handlebodies | doi=10.2307/2033843 | mr = 0173241 | year=1965 | journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume=16 | pages=192–195 | jstor=2033843 | issue=2| doi-access=free }}</ref> it remains open. Together with [[Gustav A. Hedlund]] and [[Roger Lyndon]], he proved the [[Curtis–Hedlund–Lyndon theorem]] characterizing [[cellular automata]] as being defined by [[continuous function|continuous]] [[equivariant]] functions on a [[shift space]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Hedlund | first = Gustav A. | author-link = Gustav A. Hedlund
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01691062
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Mathematical Systems Theory
 | pages = 320–375
 | title = Endomorphisms and Automorphisms of the Shift Dynamical Systems
 | volume = 3
 | year = 1969| s2cid = 21803927 }}</ref>

Curtis was the author of two books, ''Matrix Groups'' (Springer-Verlag, 1979), and ''Abstract Linear Algebra'' (Springer-Verlag, 1990).
